books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: John Brown, address to the Virginia court (November 2, 1859)

stimulus.source_note: John Brown, address to the Virginia court, November 2, 1859, before sentencing for the Harpers Ferry raid. Public domain. Wording verified against the Gilder Lehrman transcript (Address of John Brown to the Virginia Court, GLC05508.051) and the Dickinson House Divided text. The two passages appear in this order in the address; omissions are marked.
stimulus.text: I never did intend murder, or treason, or the destruction of property, or to excite or incite slaves to rebellion, or to make insurrection. . . . I believe that to have interfered as I have done . . . in behalf of His despised poor, was not wrong, but right.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note

rationales.A: Brown says the opposite: he feels no guilt and calls his interference right.
rationales.B: Brown never sought office; he sought to free slaves and answer to God.
rationales.C: Brown calls his interference “not wrong, but right,” a judgment he frames as God’s, not man’s.
rationales.D: The speech says nothing about the tariff; Brown’s cause was slavery.
rationales.general:
1. Read Brown’s verdict on himself: his interference “was not wrong, but right.”
2. Read his standard: he acted for God’s “despised poor,” not for himself.
3. See the claim: a man who believes God commands him will not call his deed a crime.
Remember: when a speaker appeals to God over the law, he is telling you which court he answers to.
